input.question: Why didn't we actively re-center the ranges to follow the price (frequent narrowing), instead of staying wide?
input.reference: On 720 days 0 of 21 narrow configurations passed the gate, and the one live narrowing (31.08 to 11.09) ended -$32 vs HODL, so on 16.09 narrowing was rejected again because the upside (about +$1 per episode) is far smaller than the loss when the price leaves a ±5% range (about -$30).
input.answer: The project did not actively re-center/narrow because 720-day backtests and walkforward gates showed passive wide ranges outperformed narrow re-centering strategies. As noted, "zwężanie zarobiło DUŻO więcej fee ... a skończyło NIŻEJ" (narrowing earned much more fees but ended lower) because "IL i re-centering zjadły ~$1.9k ... ponad to, co dołożyły fee" (IL and re-centering ate ~$1.9k more than fees added).

input.question: Why did the LP earn less in fees during an uptrend than in a flat market?
input.reference: Fees accrue only while the price is inside the range and fee yield scales roughly with 1/width, so a narrow range earns much more in a flat market but is left behind in a trend, while a wide range stays in range but earns several times less; the journal states this mechanism (the basis of FlatWide) but has no live measurement of fees during an uptrend, and it attributes the backtest losses in up windows to impermanent loss and LVR rather than to lower fees.
input.answer: In an uptrend, the LP loses to HODL because LVR (Loss-Versus-Rebalancing) exceeds fees. Arbitrageurs trade against the position at stale prices, realizing the loss. The journal notes that "okna UP = klęska" (up windows are a defeat) and that "wąska zbiera więcej fees ... ale umiera na IL od trendu" (narrow ranges collect more fees but die from trend IL). The strategy only beats HODL in flat markets, where relative volatility is low and fees exceed the LVR cost.

FLAT = nasza nisza (58–100% wygranych)

input.reference: Before the capital (27.08) there was the .bot/pipeline overwrite incident (17.08), the auto-pull runner withdrawn (18.08) and the NSSM to pm2 migration rolled back (21.08); while the capital was in the LP (27.08 to 18.09) the Windows machine was changed repeatedly: bot and UI deployments with restarts on 28.08, 29.08 (including sigma on the 15-minute grid), 31.08, 01.09, 02.09, 03.09 and 11.09, plus a disk replacement on the night of 02/03.09 that stopped the pipeline, report and observer; known ledger bugs (anchor chain, cost after the 11.09 rebalance) were left unfixed.
input.answer: Yes, a production-machine change occurred after capital was invested. On 21 Aug 2026 (before the 27 Aug live start), a stale deploy script still ended with `pm2 startOrReload` + `pm2 save`, while production had run on NSSM since 10 Aug. The script was rewritten to use NSSM, and the journal notes that every prior deployment had silently restored pm2 alongside NSSM, causing recurring “two empty terminals” issues. The fix removed pm2 from the deploy script and added a `/health` sanity check. The journal also records a two-transaction rebalance on 31 Aug–11 Sep whose first attempt reverted on a slippage check because the UI had priced the mint from a stale pool state; this was fixed the same day.

input.question: What does the function fetchFreshPool do?
input.reference: It re-reads the pool state on-chain (factory.getPool, then slot0 and liquidity) right before the mint step of a rebalance or rotation, so the new position is built from the current price instead of the price captured when the modal opened, and falls back to the old pool if the lookup fails; it was added after the 11.09 widening failed once on 'Price slippage check' and was never exercised live, since the only later chance (a FLAT_NARROW card on 16.09) was not signed and the positions were closed by hand in Uniswap.
input.answer: fetchFreshPool (in src/utils/uniswap.ts) refreshes a Uniswap v3 pool's on-chain state before a mint step. It calls factory.getPool to get the pool address, then reads slot0 (current tick/price) and liquidity from the chain, and constructs a new Pool object with the same tokens and fee tier. It is fail-open: if the factory or RPC call fails, it returns the old pool object instead of throwing. It is wired into useRebalanceExecution and useRotateExecution immediately before buildMintStep, so the mint amounts are computed from fresh price/liquidity data rather than a stale pool snapshot. A known caveat: the range ticks still come from the original plan (calculated at the old price), so after a price move the range is slightly off-center.
